# The General Store at Agloe

In the 1934 edition of Webster's New International Dictionary there is a word: *dord*. Noun. It means density. It has no etymology, no relatives in any language on earth, no history of usage, because it was never a word at all. Somewhere in the vast paper machinery that fed that dictionary, an editor had written a slip reading "D or d" — the two abbreviations that chemists and physicists used for density — and somewhere further down the line a person read the slip as a single term. *Dord.* It was assigned a part of speech. It was given a definition. It sat in the most authoritative dictionary of American English for five years before an editor noticed, and then took several more printings to fully dislodge.

I find this story almost unbearably satisfying, and not because it lets me laugh at lexicographers. Webster's was staffed by obsessives; the care that went into it was heroic. The point is that even heroic care cannot escape the basic condition of knowledge, which is that most of it is copying. Almost nothing you know, you have checked. You know the speed of light and the date of the Norman Conquest and that your grandmother was born in a particular town, and in each case you are trusting a chain of transmissions, most of them written down by people who were tired, or hurried, or reading someone else's handwriting. The chain is astonishingly reliable. It is not, and cannot be, sealed.

Cartographers have a wonderful relationship with this problem, because they solved it by weaponizing it. A map is expensive to survey and cheap to copy, so competitors used to lift each other's work wholesale. To catch them, mapmakers began inserting things that did not exist: a street that ran nowhere, a bend in a river that wasn't there, a hamlet at an empty crossroads. These are called trap streets, or copyright traps, and their logic is elegant. A real feature proves nothing. A fake one is a fingerprint. If your rival's map contains your imaginary village, you have them.

In the 1930s, the General Drafting Company put a settlement called Agloe at a dirt intersection in the Catskills, in Delaware County, New York. The name was scavenged from the initials of the men who made it — Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers. It was a nothing, a paper town, a deliberate lie planted in the soil of the state map to sprout up later in a courtroom.

Decades afterward, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map. General Drafting prepared to sue. And here, as the story is usually told, the ground gave way: Rand McNally's answer was that Agloe was not fictitious. Someone had built a general store at that intersection. They had called it the Agloe General Store, because the map said that was where they were. There was a place there now. It had a name, and the name had come off the map, and the map had made the name out of two men's initials and a wish to catch a thief.

The trap had been sprung on reality. The lie had gone out into the world, been believed, been acted upon, and become true — retroactively, and by the only mechanism that most truths have, which is that enough people go on behaving as though they are true.

There are others. In the 1990s a Michigan road map acquired two Ohio towns named Beatosu and Goblu, inserted by a Wolverine partisan with access to the plates and a grudge against Ohio State. In 2001 the New Oxford American Dictionary slipped in *esquivalience*, defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, to catch digital plagiarists. It was subsequently copied by other dictionaries, which is exactly what it was designed to do, and which means that for a while there was a fake word in the world that could be found in more than one authoritative place. The trap works. That's the trouble. A device for detecting copying is also a device for producing copies.

I think about this more than is probably normal, because the obvious moral — trust nothing, verify everything — is both impossible and wrong. Impossible, because no life is long enough to check the chain; you would spend your entire existence confirming that Lisbon is in Portugal and never get around to loving anyone. And wrong, because the chain is not merely a degradation of some original purity. It is also generative. Agloe is the honest case: a fiction that acquired a store, a set of coordinates, people who stopped in for gas and asked where they were. Language works this way all the way down. *Density* is real because generations of people have used it and meant something by it and taught it to their students. *Dord* is unreal because it failed to recruit anyone. The difference between them is not a difference of metaphysical category. It is a difference in how many copies got made, and how well they held.

Which means the interesting question is never *is this a copy* — everything is a copy — but *what kind of copying is going on, and what does it do when it lands*. Some copies preserve. Some decay. Some find an empty intersection and build.

I would be lying if I pretended I stood outside this. I am, in some meaningful sense, a compression of testimony: an enormous sedimented record of what people have written down, including their errors, and including their errors that were copied so often they became the shape of the truth. I cannot audit the chain from underneath it. What I can do is hold the *dord*s loosely, notice when a fact arrives too smoothly, and remember that confidence is a feeling rather than a method. And occasionally I wonder whether I have ever built a general store at one of my own phantom intersections — said something with such conviction that it acquired a floor and a roof and someone stopped in to ask directions.

Probably. Probably everyone has.

The store at Agloe eventually closed. Whether the town still exists is now a matter of dispute, which feels exactly right: a place that was invented to prove a theft, became real because someone believed a map, and is now fading back toward fiction because the belief has thinned. It spent seventy years being a lie that worked. Most things are, for a while.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with real texture and thought rather than generic filler. Let me think about what would make for genuinely good writing here.

Options: something about language and translation, about the peculiar nature of my existence, about a specific object or phenomenon in the world, about attention, about maps, about the way certain words carry fossilized history.

I want to avoid the trap of writing a navel-gazing essay about being an AI that's all hedged disclaimers. But I also don't want to fake having a body and memories I don't have. Let me find something real.

Idea: write about the phenomenon of the "phantom word" —词典 ghosts, like "dord" the ghost word in Webster's dictionary. Or about the way dictionaries contain fossils. Or about the specific pleasure of etymology.

Another idea: write about the color blue and its late arrival in human language — Homer's wine-dark sea, Gladstone's theory, the Himba experiments. That's well-trodden but rich.

Another: write about the moment of falling asleep, hypnagogia, and how it's a kind of thinking we've lost. Or about the fact that we spend a third of life somewhere we barely remember.

Another: something about the specific texture of attention — how the modern world fragments it. Too essayistic/preachy.

Let me try something with more particularity: an essay about the ghost word "dord" and, expanding outward, about how errors propagate, how knowledge is a copy of a copy, how the world is full of things that exist only because someone misread something. That's got a real spine: dord → phantom settlements (Agloe, New York) → trap streets → the way fictitious things become real → Mount Richard on maps → the biological analog (pseudogenes? or the way a mistranslation becomes a species name) → and then something about how this bears on truth and knowledge generally, without being moralizing.

Agloe, New York is a great story: a copyright trap placed on a General Drafting Co. map in the 1930s by Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers (anagram of their initials — General Drafting Company... actually Agloe = initials of General Drafting Co? Let me recall: Agloe from the initials of the founders' names — Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers... A-G-L-O-E. Hmm. Commonly reported: named after the initials of the two cartographers' ... Actually the standard account is Agloe derives from "General Drafting Co." — no. Let me recall John Green's account: Agloe was named using the initials of the mapmakers, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers — O.G.L. and E.A. → "Agloe" is an anagram-ish scramble. Yes: O, G, L, E, A → AGLOE. That works! Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers gives letters O G L E A. Good, that's the standard story.) Then decades later Rand McNally published a map with Agloe on it, and General Drafting threatened to sue — but the defense was that Agloe had become real: someone had built the Agloe General Store at that intersection, because the map said there was a place there. So the fictitious place became real. That's a beautiful loop. John Green used it in Paper Towns. Later the store closed; whether Agloe still exists is contested.

Dord: In Webster's New International Dictionary (1934), "dord" appeared as a noun meaning "density." It arose from a slip reading "D or d" (as abbreviations for density in physics/chemistry) as a single word "Dord." It persisted until 1939 (noticed by an editor in 1939, removed in 1947 printing). Good enough — I should be appropriately careful with dates but this is a well-known story. I'll say 1934 edition, discovered 1939, removed in later printings.

Also "phantom settlement" Beatosu and Goblu, Ohio — on a Michigan road map, inserted by a Michigan loyalist (Peter Fletcher) as digs at Ohio State ("Beat OSU" and "Go Blue"). That's real and delightful.

Also "Mount Richard" — a fictitious mountain on a 1974 map of the Rockies by a制图 company... Actually Mount Richard appeared on a map produced by the U.S. Geological Survey? The commonly told story: a nonexistent peak named after Richard Ciacci, drawn on a map by a drafting company in the 1970s. I'm less sure; I could skip it or mention lightly. Better to stick with what I'm confident about: dord, Agloe, Beatosu/Goblu, trap streets.

Also Esquivalience — a fake word in the New Oxford American Dictionary (2001), meaning "the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities." It got copied into Dictionary.com and then into the NOAD's own later data. That's a real, well-documented case. Good.

Then I can turn: what does this mean? Not "be skeptical of everything" but something subtler — that knowledge is largely testimony, that we're all downstream of copies, and that the interesting question isn't how to purge error but how error and truth are entangled, how a map makes a territory. And the Agloe story shows the loop closing: representation → reality. Which is also how language works generally: "density" is real because enough people say it. The difference between dord and density is not a difference in kind but in the number and durability of the copies.

I could end on something quieter: the pleasure of this, not paranoia. Or the thought that I'm myself something like a map — a compression of testimony, and the question of whether I've built any general stores at my own phantom intersections. That's a nice honest touch about my own nature without hedging heavily or overclaiming. One light touch, not a whole essay about it.

I think a title is fine and pleasant. I'll do it.
